title: Drop The Strength That Earned You The Promotion
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (www.theartofaskingquestions.com), September 19, 2026
summary: Chiarelli, writing with executive coach Amanda Breckenridge, argues that a promotion is not simply an invitation to do more of what already worked. The strength that made someone visible at one level, whether technical mastery, operational fluency, or a talent for keeping everyone aligned, tends to become a constraint at the next, and the piece frames each step up as a trade rather than an addition: mastery for multiplication, fluency for selection, cohesion for conviction, service for authority. Drawing on 360 assessment data from more than forty senior leaders and coaching work with over two hundred clients, the authors describe three competing identities inside the same person, the doer, the accommodator, and the newer strategic leader, and note that the first two can quietly become ways of avoiding the harder work of deciding and holding a position. The central diagnosis is that organisations describe what a new role adds but almost never describe what it should end, so leaders carry every old habit forward until they are effectively doing several jobs at once. The article closes by reframing the standard promotion question, urging leaders to ask not only what they must start doing but what someone or something else now needs to take over.
points: The piece treats each promotion as a trade rather than an accumulation, naming four specific swaps including mastery for multiplication and cohesion for conviction.
It argues the problem survives self-awareness, because under pressure the strength practised longest is the one that fires first.
Breckenridge's 360 data and coaching notes are used to identify three competing identities in one leader, the doer, the accommodator, and the strategic leader.
The authors blame organisations for describing what a role adds while staying silent on what it should retire, which leaves leaders carrying everything.
The practical move offered is a second question at promotion time about what another person or system should now take over.
quotes: Then you arrive at the next level and discover something quite uncomfortable: the strength that got you there is not necessarily the strength that will make you successful now. In fact, you may need to stop leading with it.
If you cannot name the strength you are putting down as you step up in your next role, there is a good chance you have simply added another one to an ever-growing toolkit.
As your responsibility increases, however, success may depend less on your own mastery and more on what you enable around you. The trade is mastery for multiplication.
These transitions do not mean that your 'old' strengths have become worthless, and that is exactly what makes things difficult: the strength still works.
There is another problem: organisations are usually much better at describing what comes next than what comes to an end.

But when you are in leadership, the doer and accommodator identities can also become ways of avoiding the harder work of deciding, holding a position and allowing other people to carry responsibility.
The hardest part of a promotion may be accepting that some of what made you successful has to become less important.
But the transition usually involves a period where the strengths that made you successful start producing diminishing returns.
